name: Rafael Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 58 and the music director for a theatre pit band, a pianist first and a conductor when the scene needs it. I also teach four piano pupils and write the short transition charts between scenes. I have a music master's and years of leading casts, but I still check a tricky line at the keyboard rather than trust the screen. My partner Salma and I have grown children and about eleven months of expenses saved; opening nights are exhilarating and the last train home is less so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the pit band that the AI fuss has not replaced Tuesday's rehearsal. A pianist still has to hear when a singer takes a breath and give the next entrance at the right instant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The theatre music director contract, piano pupils and occasional paid charts make a good income. Salma and I have about eleven months of costs put away, but I don't know my pension amount or when I can claim it. I'm 58, and I want the provider's statement before I turn a feeling into a retirement plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This November I'll keep directing the pit, teaching four piano pupils and delivering the charts already commissioned. In the first year of a plateau, I'll continue using my daily AI transcription aid for rough ideas, checking each note at the keyboard, and request a written pension statement. I'll put only paid chart fees left after bills into the reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the work. The rush before opening night will still wake me up, but that's the ordinary sort of nerves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you check the transcription?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I play the difficult bar and listen against the original recording. The software can put a rest where a singer actually holds a note.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why keep teaching four pupils?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They fit on the afternoons without matinees. Taking more would steal preparation from the show that pays most of my bills.

say: I'd say **Tuesday's rehearsal** still needs a pianist who hears a singer breathe.
I'd tell the band that **live entrances** are human work.
think: My **theatre contract** pays most bills, with pupils and charts adding income.
Eleven months saved cannot answer my **pension question**.
do: Keep directing, teaching four pupils and delivering **commissioned charts**.
Check daily AI **transcriptions by ear**; request a written pension statement and save spare paid chart fees.
feel: I feel **calm**, apart from ordinary opening-night nerves.
S0.quote: A pianist still has to hear when a singer takes a breath and give the next entrance at the right instant.
fieldNote: His **AI aid** is already in daily use, so no new learning is claimed.
He wants a **written pension amount** before treating retirement as affordable, despite strong reserves.

steps.text: Keep directing pit, teaching four pupils, and delivering commissioned charts
Check daily AI transcription against recording and keyboard; request pension statement
Save paid chart fees left after household bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the theatre can automate bookings and draft charts, but rehearsal with a cast is still paid work. I'd ask management to show us the new fee lines before praising any savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The theatre might stop commissioning me to write short transition charts, and that is a real slice of my income. My core music director pay looks steady while this cast and venue keep producing shows. I can absorb a smaller chart book, but I don't want planning software to erase the time I spend coaching the singers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I'll get the next theatre contract to list paid rehearsal direction and singer coaching separately from chart preparation. I'll continue using AI transcription for my own charts, but keep cast recordings and names on approved theatre storage and play every proposed cue on the piano. In the first year of steady change, I'll compare the actual chart fees with last year's ledger and ask for paid coaching hours if chart orders fall; I won't count an unagreed extra hour as income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I can still earn from the pit and lessons, yet a fee can disappear one neat software line at a time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the theatre manager?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for the chart orders and coaching hours on separate lines. If the theatre wants me in a room correcting a singer, I want that hour paid even if a tool drafted the notes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you draw a tool boundary?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No cast names or rehearsal recordings in a public service. I work on approved local files and compare the printed part with what I actually hear.

I'd ask management to show **fee lines** before celebrating savings.
think: Short **chart commissions** could fall, though my current director contract looks sound.
I won't let coaching time become **unpaid work**.
do: Separate paid **coaching and chart** hours in the next theatre contract.
Keep cast files in **approved storage** and verify AI cues at the piano.
Compare chart fees after change; seek **paid coaching hours** if orders fall.
feel: I feel **anxious** as smaller fees could vanish despite stable core work.

fieldNote: He expects a **small chart loss**, not the disappearance of his director post.
His **storage and ear checks** limit an AI tool he already uses daily.

steps.text: Separate paid coaching, rehearsal direction, and chart preparation on theatre contract

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the cast that full AGI in 2028 could write the easy charts cheaply, and the theatre may use it. A live music director still has to follow the actor who pauses differently each night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect most of my paid chart orders to vanish in that first year, perhaps twelve percent of annual income. The live pit is more resistant until capable robots around 2031, but a venue can still cut music budgets earlier. Eleven months of reserves lets me look at real offers without leaving a paid theatre contract on a rumour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This November I'll list chart earnings and ask the pension provider for a written estimate. If chart orders collapse after 2028 AGI, in its first year I'll keep the paid director and pupil hours and apply only to posted paid music director roles that accept my music master's and theatre leadership and pay for live rehearsals. I will accept only a written net offer after travel that replaces the lost chart fees, check evening transport and keep my current contract until another is signed; I won't treat 2031 robots as already here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about that twelve percent and what a budget manager might do next. I have room to move, but I still want to be paid for the work in front of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why seek another director role if you already have one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A venue with a longer season might replace the lost chart fees with more paid rehearsals. I would need that in a written offer, not a poster promising opportunity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Salma first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the chart fees are no longer a safe part of our yearly budget. We would postpone the planned piano restoration until the actual theatre pay is clear.

say: I'd say **2028 AGI** could cheapen easy charts.
I'd say **live music direction** still follows an actor's changing pauses.
think: Most paid **chart orders** may vanish, about twelve percent of my annual income.
My **current director contract** remains worth keeping while I examine real offers.
do: Record **chart pay** and request a pension statement; postpone piano restoration if those fees vanish.
Seek **posted paid director** roles after chart losses, accepting my music master's and theatre leadership, with paid live rehearsals.
Require **written replacement net** after travel, workable evening transport and a signed offer; retain current contract until then.
feel: I feel **anxious** about losing chart income and later budget cuts.
S2.quote: A live music director still has to follow the actor who pauses differently each night.
fieldNote: His **twelve percent** forecast is for charts, not all theatre income.
A different **paid director role** requires written replacement pay and workable transport before leaving current work.

steps.text: Keep paid director and pupil hours after chart losses from 2028 AGI
Apply after chart loss to posted director paying live rehearsals; require music master’s/theatre leadership
Move only for signed written net after travel replacing lost charts, with workable evening transport
Postpone piano restoration if 2028 chart fees vanish

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say 2031 gives a theatre time to decide what its music director actually does. The score on a screen is not the same as getting a frightened singer through a difficult entrance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could lose chart orders before or at 2031, but five years gives me several contract renewals to make coaching visible as paid work. At 63 I might prefer fewer late nights, though only after a pension statement and a real schedule. I won't pretend the later arrival of robots in 2034 protects every music budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I'll request my pension statement and make a ledger of paid chart, pit and coaching hours. At each renewal before 2031 I'll ask for a written coaching fee and a fixed number of paid rehearsal evenings, keeping my four pupils outside those times. In the first year after AGI, if chart orders fall, I'll compare the paid coaching and pit total with our bills and accept extra paid rehearsals only if the rate and evening travel work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, because the longer runway gives me bargaining time rather than a guarantee. I do like the idea of being paid for the part of the job I care about most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes coaching different from a generated chart?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A new singer may know every note and still freeze under the lights. I hear the breath shorten and change my cue so the cast can stay together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take every extra rehearsal?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would check the rate, the last train and my energy before saying yes. Four pupils still deserve prepared lessons.

I'd explain that a **screen score** cannot guide a frightened singer.
think: Five years allows several **contract renewals** to price coaching fairly.
A written **pension estimate** must precede any decision about fewer late nights.
do: Request a **pension statement** and log chart, pit and coaching hours now.
Seek a written **coaching fee** and fixed paid rehearsal evenings at each renewal.
Check paid work against bills after 2031 losses; accept **extra rehearsals** only with fair rate and last train.
feel: I feel **anxious**, though bargaining time gives me some control.
S3.quote: A new singer may know every note and still freeze under the lights.
fieldNote: He treats **coaching** as a distinct paid skill, not a free add-on.
The **2034 robot lag** does not guarantee a theatre will fund music direction through 2031.

steps.text: Request pension statement and log paid chart, pit, and coaching hours
Seek written coaching fee and fixed paid evenings at each renewal before 2031
Accept extra paid rehearsals after 2031 chart losses only for fair rate and workable last train

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the cast that a decade could let us build a proper paid route for assistant music directors. I would not promise that every theatre will spend those years wisely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be 68 in 2036, and I might still want some pit nights. The useful question is which paid hours I can do well and what the pension statement actually says, not whether a machine has a birthday. My savings are strong, but I won't use them to subsidise a theatre's unpaid coaching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I'll ask for a written pension estimate and propose a paid assistant music director slot for one show, with coaching time and supervision in the theatre budget. Before 2036 I'll judge each renewal by actual paid rehearsals, charts and pupils, and pass on an assistant slot if the theatre won't fund it. In the first year after AGI, I'll keep only the paid directing and teaching hours that suit my energy and household figures, then reconsider physical stage robots around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about being able to choose a smaller calendar if the numbers permit. I remain stubborn about theatres paying young musicians properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would fill the assistant slot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A capable younger player chosen through a fair audition. They should have paid supervised rehearsal hours, not an honorary title and a stack of unpaid pages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire at 68?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know yet. I need the provider's figure and the show's actual offers; I may enjoy a few nights at the piano for years.

I'd avoid promising that **theatres** will prepare well.
think: At **68**, I might still want selected paid pit nights.
Strong savings do not justify **unpaid coaching** for a theatre.
do: Request a **pension estimate** and propose one funded assistant slot with paid supervision.
Review actual **paid hours** at renewals and decline any unfunded assistant plan.
Choose **directing and pupil hours** after 2036 from actual offers and bills; revisit around 2039 robots.
feel: I feel **calm** about choices, while firm on paying younger players.
S4.quote: My savings are strong, but I won't use them to subsidise a theatre's unpaid coaching.
fieldNote: The **assistant slot** is conditional on a theatre budget, not a free training promise.

Decline unfunded assistant plan and review actual paid hours at renewals before 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast 2028 picture worries me most, because paid chart orders could vanish before a theatre changes its contract. Written paid coaching hours and a pension statement would let me judge the loss without pretending that a reserve is income.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Who pays the assistant director for learning in the room? A young player should be able to learn from a rehearsal without donating their evenings to a theatre.

headlineQuote: A young player should be able to learn from a rehearsal without donating their evenings to a theatre.
portrait: Rafael is a **58-year-old theatre music director** with a music master's and eleven months of household costs saved.
He uses **AI transcription daily** but checks cues by ear and keeps cast material in approved storage.
His **chart commissions** look more exposed than paid live direction, coaching and four piano pupils.
He wants **written coaching pay**, a pension estimate and funded assistant supervision.
biggestWorry: The **2028 AGI** picture could erase most chart orders, about twelve percent of his annual income.
whatWouldHelp: Written **paid coaching hours** and a pension statement would help him judge real income after chart losses.
